newsitem.title: UK: Segers paid in large cash sums after side lost.
newsitem.headline: Segers paid in large cash sums after side lost.

text.p: Former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, charged with fixing matches for an Asian betting syndicate, regularly paid large sums of cash into a Swiss bank account after his side lost, a court heard on Thursday.

Chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith told a court in the southern English town of Winchester that Segers had made seven deposits totalling 104,000 pounds ($174,600) into the bank's London branch from October 1993 to November 1994.

During this period the team lost 14 premier league games in which Segers played in goal, including the crucial last match of the 1993/94 season when Everton maintained their premier league place by beating Wimbledon 3-2 after trailing 2-0.

The prosecution accuses Segers of rigging games and says he was paid by former striker John Fashanu -- who it said could not explain why he had received more than 250,000 pounds from Indonesia -- and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim.
All three plead not guilty. Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar faces separate match-rigging charges along with Fashanu and Lim. Grobbelaar has also pleaded not guilty.

Calvert Smith finished summing up his case, which will reopen next Monday when chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent -- who made covert recordings of Grobbelaar admitting he had taken money to fix matches -- takes the stand.

The prosecutor, who described the technical details of the case as "mind-boggling" and apologised for inflicting pain on those present in the courtroom, took the jury through the many dozens of phone calls the three defendants made.
He said Segers, Fashanu and Lim had been in regular contact before each game that Wimbledon lost and said Lim had called numbers in Indonesia just before and just after each game.
Segers said he only talked to Fashanu infrequently but phone logs showed the two men called each other countless times during the period in question.
"Here are the multiplicitous contacts about which Segers lied, here are the games that Wimbledon lost and here are the calls around those matches," Calvert Smith told the jury.
"Can you draw the inference, as we would like you to do, that the money, telephone calls and matches are linked?"

Calvert Smith said it was no coincidence that there had been a flurry of calls between the defendants after the Sun newspaper confronted Grobbelaar on November 8, 1984, and accused him of fixing matches.
"We suggest that it's obvious there was a great deal of fluttering in the dovecotes after the news became public," he told the jury. Contacts between the four then tailed off.

Segers paid in five seperate amounts of cash during the 1993 and 1994 seasons totalling 65,000 pounds, the last being a 19,000 pounds deposit just after the 3-2 loss to Everton. Shortly afterwards he bought 70,000 pounds worth of bonds.

When first interviewed by police in 1995 Segers told police that the money came from car thefts he had carried out in the Netherlands when younger, but Calvert Smith dismissed the explanation as totally far-fetched.
Segers paid in no more money until 19,000 pounds he deposited at the end of October, after a miserable run in which Wimbledon lost four games in a row.
On November 7, just one day before the Sun newspaper broke the story, Segers paid in another 20,000 pounds. Two days earlier the side had lost 3-1 to Leeds.
On Wednesday Calvert Smith quoted Grobbelaar as saying in a covert recording that the Far Eastern syndicate chose in advance the matches which they wanted rigged.

"We suggest that the proximity of the back-to-back calls to soccer matches is significant. What was going on was a constant process of "Shall we go with this one or wait till next Saturday'?" he told the court. ($1=.5958 Pound)
